Sister Sabria: La passion d’aider: Sister Sabria: The Passion for Helping
Depuis 40 ans, sœur Sabria aide les plus: For 40 years, Sister Sabria has been helping Montréal’s most vulnerable. More than 700,000 meals distributed and hundreds of families supported.
Sabariah Binti Hussein, mieux connue sou: Sabariah Binti Hussein, better known as Sister Sabria. Photo credit: Labib Benslama
Il y a 40 ans, Sabariah Binti Hussein, m: Forty years ago, Sabariah Binti Hussein, better known as Sister Sabria, landed in Montréal after answering a job posting for a teacher of children with special needs. “Given my experience, I think I was the ideal candidate,” she says.
Celle qu’on surnomme « la mère Teresa de: Nicknamed “the Mother Teresa of Montréal,” she was looking for a change of scenery at the time. “My father and mother had passed away. I felt a little alone. I really wanted to go somewhere else, because my sisters had gotten married and I was going to be left on my own. And I don’t like that. So I could be more adventurous if I went abroad, and gain more experience,” she says.
Déjà à l’époque, dans sa Malaisie natale: Even back then, in her native Malaysia, Sister Sabria knew her way around a stove. “I worked in a restaurant, I cooked Western dishes in Kuala Lumpur,” she says.
Dès son arrivée à Montréal, sœur Sabria: As soon as she arrived in Montréal, Sister Sabria threw herself into her work teaching children. She soon met the man who would become her partner. “I was living with my mother-in-law,” she remembers. “I started working, then helping those in need. My mother-in-law asked me: ‘Who are these sandwiches for? There are only three of us, but you’re making a lot.’”
Sœur Sabria lui confie alors son secret: Sister Sabria then confided her secret: it was to feed the homeless. “She was so happy that she told me: ‘Okay! Next time, I’ll make the soup, and you make the sandwiches!’” she recalls. “She taught me how to make soup the French way, the Canadian way. That’s how I got to know the tastes of people experiencing homelessness.”
Par la suite, sœur Sabria s’installe dan: Afterward, Sister Sabria settled in the Notre-Dame-de-Grâce neighbourhood and joined the mosque of the Communauté musulmane du Québec (CMQ). “I got to know more and more people, and I met many Muslims who needed help too,” she explains.
Une anecdote résume bien son caractère –: One anecdote sums up her character – and her selflessness. “I remember very well the furniture my husband had bought and that I had given away. The second time, I did the same thing, I gave away new furniture, brand new. So he was left without furniture for about a year, even two,” she remembers. There was nothing to sit on. “So I told him: ‘I think I’m not in the right place.’ My husband was fed up with me!”
L'enseignante transforme alors son appar: The teacher then turned her apartment into a self-serve help counter. “Where we had all our shelves, instead of books, I put clothes so people could come and pick them up. I also started giving out food items like oil, flour, sugar, and all that. I laid them out so they could take them easily, like in a grocery store, but without having to pay,” says the helper.
Au fil du temps, sœur Sabria fait la con: Over time, Sister Sabria got to know several families in need. She set to work, notably <l1>in collaboration with the leadership of the Montréal chapter of the Canadian Council of Muslim Women</l1>.
Ce n’est que le début d’une série de col: This was only the start of a series of collaborations with other organizations, for other causes. This year, for example, the Sister Sabria Foundation teamed up with <l1>Human Concern International</l1> to distribute winter coats and boots to children. “Very often, every month, there’s always another organization that supports us, that helps us make a project or a program a success,” says Sister Sabria, delighted.
En 2017, des collaborateurs lui suggèren: In 2017, collaborators suggested she create a foundation to carry the project forward. “They proposed the name ‘Sister Sabria Foundation,’ which I totally disagreed with at first. But they explained that they had chosen that name because more and more people wanted to know who was behind the project,” says the woman who doesn’t like to draw attention to herself.
Bientôt, l’organisme fait l'acquisition: Soon, the organization acquired a building at 5271 Saint-Hubert Street in Montréal. That way, says the founder, the organization can reach even more people. “To date, we have been able to house 400 people and families,” says the woman who also founded a shelter for women. The foundation runs several programs that help vulnerable people. In almost 40 years, more than 700,000 meals have been distributed and hundreds of thousands of dollars have been raised to support various causes.
La Sister Sabria Foundation, c’est égale: The Sister Sabria Foundation is also a large team of volunteers from different backgrounds. “There are Tunisians, Algerians, Moroccans. There are also Asians who join us, as well as Palestinians, and even Iraqis. We have sent help to various households of different origins,” says Sister Sabria.
Avant tout, ce sont les liens qui se tis: Above all, it’s the bonds that form that make it possible to do more. “Alhamdulillah, they accept me as I am, even though I can sometimes be unpleasant,” the founder apologizes. “Sometimes it’s so hectic that we don’t have time to think.”
Cependant, les relations tissées restent: Still, the relationships she has built remain strong. “Our friendship is so strong! I truly appreciate their kindness and warmth. The bond that unites us is like the one between a mother and her children,” she says of her team.
À maintenant 78 ans, sœur Sabria a l’âge: Now 78, Sister Sabria is old enough to be a grandmother. Yet “sister” is still the title that suits her best. “Personally, I find that when people call me ‘sister,’ my heart softens, grows younger. If people called me ‘grandmother,’ I don’t think I could do the work as well; I would feel very old. I feel younger, and I can work with the younger generations,” she says happily.
Aujourd’hui, c’est cet amour pour la jeu: Today, it’s this love for young people that motivates her every day. “The strength that allows me to keep going is, among other things, the love I receive from the encouragement of the younger generation,” she insists. The next generation itself often comes from those who came before. “Some stay in touch, for example students from McGill and Concordia. Their children join them. They keep contacting me, with new energy, Inshallah with a younger generation,” says Sister Sabria.
Tant mieux, car pour elle, le travail es: All the better, because for her, the work is far from over. “I want to do more. And it’s never enough,” says the woman who is nowhere near done giving. She encourages everyone to do the same. “We must play our part as a society in Montréal. I think we have to do more than that. As a society, as a Muslim community, we can support one another by putting more programs in place,” says the founder.
Un conseil ? « Même si vous n’avez pas a: Any advice? “Even if you don’t have enough, give, give anyway, because Allah will help you. And I always think about the gratitude I feel about that. When I give, I receive more. When I give again, I receive more than I expected,” says Sister Sabria.
« Vous savez, je réalise à peine que cel: “You know, I’m only just realizing that it has become part of me and an integral part of my life. So I think that means that in the end, I will always want to give, even with my last breath, at the end, at the moment of my death,” says the benefactor, who is dealing with health problems.
« Pensez ainsi à l’avenir : “Plus vous d: “So think about the future this way: ‘The more you give, the more you receive, the more you think of others.’ And the more you think of others, the more people will help you. Inshallah!”
